# A Bench With Somewhere to Be

The first time the bench moved, everyone blamed the students.

It had stood outside the municipal library for thirty-seven years, facing a sycamore tree and, beyond that, a bakery whose owners changed more frequently than its sign. On Monday morning, it was discovered two streets away, beside a bus stop that had no shelter. An elderly woman was sitting on it with a shopping bag between her shoes.

“Very thoughtful,” she told the man who came to retrieve it.

The man’s name was Leon. He worked for the Department of Streets and Public Furniture, a title that made his brother laugh every Christmas.

Leon examined the bench before loading it onto his truck. It was ordinary: five wooden slats, two cast-iron ends, a brass plaque dedicated to someone called Edith Bell. One armrest had been polished smooth by decades of hands. Underneath, among fossilized chewing gum and several ambitious declarations of love, someone had written THIS IS NOT THE END in green marker.

There were no wheels, no ropes, and no marks suggesting it had been dragged.

Leon called his supervisor.

“Students,” she said.

“That’s what I thought.”

“Then why are you calling?”

He returned the bench to the library.

***

On Thursday, it was outside the maternity clinic.

On Saturday, it appeared halfway up Bellwether Hill, where people regularly underestimated the slope. On Sunday morning, a jogger found it beside the river, facing the water rather than the path.

Each time, Leon brought it back.

He began doing this before his other assignments, partly because the truck was already empty and partly because he disliked imagining someone looking for a familiar place to sit and finding only four pale rectangles on the pavement.

The librarian, Mrs. Vale, watched him unload it for the fourth time.

“Perhaps Edith liked a change of scene,” she said.

“Did you know her?”

“No. But I’ve become acquainted with her bench.”

Leon checked the municipal records. Edith Bell had taught geography at the secondary school. The bench had been donated by former pupils after her retirement. She had lived another sixteen years and apparently spent much of that time traveling.

There was a photograph attached to the original application: Edith on a camel, wearing enormous sunglasses, looking unimpressed by whoever held the camera.

Leon printed the photograph and left it on his desk.

He did not believe in haunted furniture. He believed in loose bolts, misplaced paperwork, and people who said they had reported a broken streetlight when they had merely complained about it at dinner.

Nevertheless, he stopped calling the bench “it” quite so automatically.

***

After its sixth disappearance, his supervisor ordered him to bolt it down.

Her name was Anika Moss. She had inherited a department with three employees, two functioning vehicles, and responsibility for every public object nobody else wished to claim. She was not an unimaginative woman. She was a woman with a budget.

“People are posting photographs,” she said. “Someone has made it an account.”

“What kind of account?”

“An internet account, Leon. It has opinions about pedestrian access.”

He looked at her screen. The bench’s latest post read: SOME OF US ARE TRYING TO MAKE THIS CITY WALKABLE.

“That could be anyone,” he said.

“Precisely. Bolt it down.”

He took a drill, four heavy brackets, and a bag of anchor bolts to the library. The morning was bright. A child watched from the steps while Leon measured the distance between the bench’s feet.

“Does that hurt?” the child asked.

“The bench?”

The child nodded.

“No.”

“How do you know?”

Leon opened his mouth, then shut it.

The child’s father called from inside, and she disappeared before he had to settle the question.

He installed three brackets. At the fourth, he discovered a split in the wood beneath the seat, narrow but deep. It should have been repaired years ago. He sat back on his heels and pressed his thumb along the grain.

“Well,” he said. “That won’t do.”

Instead of bolting down the last foot, he loaded the bench onto his truck and took it to the workshop.

***

The workshop stood behind the recycling center, where the city’s ambitions arrived eventually as bent metal.

Leon liked it there. Things were allowed to be unfinished without anyone mistaking them for failures. A damaged sign lay beside a repaired gate. A drawer contained handles waiting for drawers. On the wall hung a clock that lost seven minutes every day, providing regular employment for the person assigned to correct it.

He removed the cracked slat, cut a replacement from seasoned oak, and sanded it until the edges were comfortable beneath his palm.

“You’ve been busy,” he told the bench.

The bench gave no sign of agreeing.

“My left knee isn’t what it was either.”

Outside, a loader tipped bottles into a container. The crash sounded briefly like applause.

He worked late, applying oil to the new wood and tightening the joints. When he finished, the bench looked unevenly young: four weathered slats and one golden replacement.

Leon considered staining the new piece to match. Then he decided against it. There was nothing wrong with a repair being visible.

He swept the floor, locked the workshop, and went home.

The next morning, the bench was gone.

The doors were still locked. The windows were intact.

On the floor, in a thin drift of sawdust, were four small impressions leading toward the wall.

Leon stood looking at them for a long time.

Then he called Anika.

“You should come down,” he said.

***

She arrived carrying coffee and the expression of someone determined not to have an interesting morning.

Leon showed her the empty space, the locked doors, and the tracks.

“Could be a prank.”

“Yes.”

“Could be someone with a key.”

“Yes.”

“Could be you.”

“It could.”

She looked at him.

“Is it?”

“No.”

They drank their coffee.

Eventually, Anika crouched beside the tracks. They were not footprints exactly. Each was the narrow, curved impression of an iron bench leg. They crossed the sawdust in an awkward alternating pattern, as though whatever made them was learning a difficult dance.

At the wall, they stopped.

Anika touched the plaster.

“I don’t have a procedure for this,” she said.

“That’s probably sensible.”

By noon, the bench had been found outside the employment office.

A man in a suit was eating a sandwich on it. Beside him, a woman was crying quietly into her phone.

Leon parked across the street. He watched the man offer her a paper napkin without interrupting his lunch.

For the first time, Leon did not immediately retrieve the bench.

He waited until both people had gone.

***

News traveled faster after that.

There were photographs, theories, and a short interview with a local historian who described the bench as “consistent with the district’s tradition of civic eccentricity,” which meant nothing but sounded reassuring.

Someone tied balloons to it.

Someone left flowers.

Someone attempted to sit on it for forty-eight hours, hoping to be transported somewhere meaningful. He lasted until shortly after midnight, when rain began falling and his girlfriend arrived in a taxi.

The bench remained stubbornly motionless whenever anyone watched.

It traveled only between observations, which made it difficult to film and impossible to insure.

Anika received emails from the mayor’s office, the legal department, and a company offering to sponsor the bench if its movements could be confined to commercially advantageous locations.

She deleted the last one with unusual force.

The trouble began when the bench appeared in a loading bay behind the central market.

It blocked a delivery van. The driver, already late, tried moving it alone and strained his back.

By afternoon, a complaint had become a report. By evening, the report had acquired the word liability.

The next morning, Anika showed Leon an instruction from above.

The bench was to be removed from public circulation pending assessment.

“What assessment?” he asked.

“That,” she said, “has not been assessed.”

***

They found it outside a shuttered cinema.

An old man was sitting beneath the faded posters, holding two takeaway coffees.

Leon recognized him vaguely. He had once sold newspapers from a kiosk near the station, before the kiosk became a machine selling phone chargers.

“Morning,” Leon said.

The man nodded.

“Mind if we take the bench when you’re finished?”

“Where to?”

“Storage.”

The man considered this.

“Everything goes there eventually.”

He lifted one coffee, then seemed to remember something and set it back down.

Leon looked away.

Across the road, Anika waited beside the truck. She had brought straps, wheel chocks, and a portable security camera purchased with money intended for replacement litter bins.

The old man stayed another twenty minutes.

When he left, he took both coffees.

They loaded the bench without speaking.

At the depot, they placed it inside an unused shipping container. Anika fastened a numbered seal across the doors.

“It’s temporary,” she said.

Leon nodded, although neither of them was looking at the other.

***

For three nights, nothing happened.

The security camera recorded rain, a fox, and Leon arriving earlier than necessary.

On the fourth morning, the bench was still inside the container, but its new slat had split.

Not badly. Just a fine crack along the grain.

Leon ran his finger over it.

Wood moved. He knew that. It expanded and contracted with humidity. Good timber could check in poor conditions, especially inside a steel box.

There was a perfectly reasonable explanation.

He brought in a thermometer, checked the ventilation, and moved the bench away from the wall.

The next day, another slat had cracked.

By Friday, the brass plaque had fallen off.

Leon picked it up from the floor. Edith Bell’s name sat cool and solid against his palm.

He thought of the photograph on his desk: the camel, the sunglasses, the expression of someone who had arrived somewhere and was already wondering what lay beyond it.

Then he did something unlike himself.

He went to the library and asked Mrs. Vale for help.

***

She listened without interrupting.

When he finished, she folded her hands on the desk.

“Do you want research,” she asked, “or accomplices?”

“Could we start with research?”

They spread a street map across a table.

Leon marked every place the bench had appeared. The bus stop. The clinic. Bellwether Hill. The river. The employment office. The market. The cinema.

Mrs. Vale added dates.

At first, the pattern seemed obvious: people needed somewhere to sit.

But there were already benches by the river. There were chairs inside the clinic. The market had a café.

“Perhaps it’s not just tiredness,” she said.

They looked again.

The bus stop had no shelter and a service that ran once an hour. The clinic’s waiting room closed before the final evening appointments. The market workers ate lunch on overturned crates behind the stalls.

The riverside bench nearest Edith’s chosen spot faced an advertising panel.

The cinema had closed nine months earlier.

They began making calls.

By dusk, the map was crowded with notes.

“It’s a list,” Leon said.

“Of what?”

“Places we’ve missed.”

***

Anika studied the map the next morning.

“You understand,” she said, “that I can’t submit a capital funding request on the grounds that a bench has conducted an accessibility audit.”

“Don’t mention the bench.”

“They will recognize the locations.”

“Say we conducted it.”

“That would require us to conduct it.”

Leon waited.

She sighed.

“Get your coat.”

They spent the next week walking.

They walked with an older residents’ group, with parents pushing buggies, with a woman who used crutches and knew more about the city’s gradients than its planning department.

They timed distances between seats. They noted which benches had backs, which had arms, which were surrounded by puddles, and which became too hot to touch in summer.

Leon learned that two hundred yards could be trivial or enormous.

Anika learned that a decorative stone cube outside the courthouse was not, despite its official classification, an adequate resting place.

They both learned how often people planned entire journeys around the availability of a seat.

On Friday, they submitted a report.

It contained no supernatural claims.

It did contain photographs, measurements, repair estimates, and a sentence Anika rewrote six times before allowing it to remain:

A public place is not fully public if some people cannot comfortably stay there.

***

The funding was modest.

Funding usually was.

Still, they repaired six benches, installed four more, and moved three that had apparently been positioned by someone with a grudge against shade.

Market traders paid for a sheltered seat behind the loading bays. The cinema’s owner agreed to leave space beneath the awning. A retired joiner volunteered two mornings a week at the workshop and spent most of that time criticizing Leon’s clamps.

Meanwhile, the container remained closed.

Leon visited every day.

He repaired the cracks, replaced two screws, and reattached Edith’s plaque. Sometimes he sat for a few minutes, listening to the metal walls tick in the sun.

When the work was finished, Anika came down to the depot with a folder.

“Temporary outdoor deployment,” she said. “Monitored. Subject to review.”

Leon read the form.

“Where?”

“The library.”

“And the bolts?”

Anika took the form back.

“There appears to be a clerical omission.”

They opened the doors.

***

The bench stayed outside the library for eleven days.

On the twelfth morning, it vanished.

Leon’s phone rang before breakfast.

For a moment, disappointment pressed against his ribs. He had wanted the repairs to mean something. He had wanted, perhaps unfairly, to be finished.

“Where?” he asked.

Mrs. Vale told him.

He drove to the edge of town, where a new housing estate ended abruptly beside an unfinished footpath.

The bench stood facing a field of waist-high grass.

A teenage boy was sitting on it, sketching the distant cranes. His bicycle lay nearby.

Leon got out of the truck.

“Good spot?” he asked.

The boy showed him the drawing. Above the roofs, an invented airship floated among the cranes.

Leon admired it, then sat at the other end and opened his notebook to a clean page. He drew the footpath, marked the bench’s position, and stayed until the boy finished shading the sky.
